lesson.title: The Variable in the Driver's Seat: Independent Variable
lesson.summary: The independent variable is the input you are free to choose for a function, the quantity that drives everything else and does not depend on any other variable in the relationship.
lesson.body:
In any function relating two variables, one of them gets to be chosen freely, and that one is called the independent variable. Its value does not depend on anything else in the relationship; it is simply picked, whether by a person, by time passing, or by some outside condition being controlled in an experiment. The independent variable is another name for the input, the value discussed earlier in this unit, viewed through the lens of cause and effect: it is the variable that causes a change, rather than the variable that results from one.

In an equation like y = 3x + 4, x is the independent variable, and in function notation, f(x), the letter written inside the parentheses, x, is always the independent variable by convention; it is the placeholder waiting to be filled with a freely chosen number. Recall that a variable, by itself, is simply a symbol standing in for a number that can change. What makes a variable independent specifically is its role inside a relationship between two variables: it is the one that gets to move first, on its own, unaffected by the other variable's value.

Think about a real situation to make this concrete. Suppose a rideshare ride costs a flat 2 dollars plus 1.5 dollars per mile traveled, giving the function C(m) = 1.5m + 2, where C is cost in dollars and m is miles traveled. Here, m, the number of miles, is the independent variable, because the rider chooses how many miles are traveled; the number of miles does not depend on the cost, but the cost absolutely depends on the number of miles. If a rider travels 6 miles, substitute m = 6: C(6) = 1.5(6) + 2 = 9 + 2 = 11, so a 6 mile ride costs 11 dollars. The 6 was chosen independently; the 11 followed from it.

On a graph, the independent variable is conventionally plotted along the horizontal axis, the x-axis, which is why domain, the set of allowable independent-variable values, is described as the left-to-right extent of a graph. This is a convention, not a law of mathematics, but it is followed consistently enough across science, statistics, and everyday graphs that recognizing it will help you read almost any chart you encounter, from a temperature-over-time graph, where time is independent, to a cost-per-item graph, where the item count is independent.

Identifying the independent variable in a word problem is often the very first step toward writing a correct function, because it tells you what to put inside the parentheses in function notation and what to label as x on a graph. Ask which quantity is being chosen, controlled, or allowed to vary freely, and which quantity only changes as a result; the first is the independent variable, and, as the next concept explores, the second is its natural partner, the dependent variable. Getting this identification right before writing a single equation will save you from mislabeling axes or mixing up which letter belongs inside the parentheses of your function notation.
